performers: Marian Anderson, contralto; San Francisco Symphony Orchestra; Pierre Monteux, conductor
intro: Marian Anderson sings “Wenn dein Mütterlein”, the third of Mahler’s Kindertotenlieder, in which a mother enters with a candle and, for an instant, the child is pictured following her. Pierre Monteux’s San Francisco players accompany her with cor anglais and low strings; Mahler leaves the violins out entirely.

sections.label: A · Cor anglais melody
sections.mNote: Bassoons play above a pizzicato cello pulse.

sections.label: A′ · Opening tune, varied
sections.mNote: Harp and double bass join the returning tune.

sections.label: Coda · Cor anglais, horns and cellos
sections.mNote: Bowed cellos and horns support the last cor anglais phrase.

cues.title: Low strings and vocal entry
cues.text: Plucked cellos mark the pulse beneath cor anglais and bassoons, and their lines keep moving as Anderson enters with the mother at the door. The violins are absent throughout. The score is marked “Schwer, dumpf” (heavy, muffled).
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460 (1905), pp. 33–35: Schwer, dumpf, opening scoring and vocal entry. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Diminutives in Rückert’s text
cues.text: The father looks to the place where his daughter’s face used to be, “dein lieb Gesichtchen” (your dear little face). Rückert used diminutives throughout the poem, from “Mütterlein” to “Töchterlein”.
cues.evidence: Rückert, Wenn dein Mütterlein, German text as set by Mahler at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kindertotenlieder#Text; our translation.

cues.title: Vocal line and accompaniment
cues.text: The vocal line follows the pattern of a nursery song and of a chanted counting rhyme. Beneath it the orchestra moves at twice the voice’s speed, in lines that recall the first song.
cues.evidence: Reinhold Kubik, Universal Edition introduction to Kindertotenlieder (autumn 2008), on song 3: children’s-song melodies, counting rhymes, and a linear accompaniment moving twice as fast as the voice and recalling the first song: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Kindertotenlieder/P0045027

cues.title: Second stanza, return of opening tune
cues.text: The opening tune returns above harp and double bass. Anderson’s second stanza adds the glimmer of the candle and the imagined child slipping into the room. Mahler repeats words and lengthens syllables so that this shorter stanza fills the musical shape of the first.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 40–46. The repeated words and syllable extensions are discussed at https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler3.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Venues and string numbers, 1905
cues.text: Mahler chose small rooms for these songs: the Kleiner Musikvereinssaal for the Vienna performances of 1905, then the Stephaniesaal in Graz. His string section had about ten first violins at most. This song has no violins.
cues.evidence: Mahler catalogue, Kindertotenlieder, scoring note: good evidence that the small venues were the composer’s own choice and that the strings were probably no more than 10, 8, 6, 6 and 4 (citing Hefling and Hilmar-Voit). Performances: Vienna 29 January and 3 February 1905, Graz 1 June 1905: https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtL.htm

cues.title: Alma Mahler on the Kindertotenlieder
cues.text: Alma Mahler could not understand how her husband could bewail the deaths of children “in the best of health and spirits” within an hour of kissing his own. She exclaimed: “For Heaven’s sake, don’t tempt Providence!” Mahler completed the cycle in the summer of 1904.
cues.evidence: Alma Mahler, Gustav Mahler: Memories and Letters, as quoted by Georg Predota, Interlude, 29 January 2019: https://interlude.hk/mahler-kindertotenlieder-premiered-today-1905/. The exclamation is also given in Michael Kennedy, Mahler (Master Musicians), Edward Seckerson, Mahler: His Life and Times (1982), and Stephen Johnson, Mahler (2007) (full-text excerpts seen); the memoir itself was not opened. Kubik dates songs 2 and 5 to 1904: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Kindertotenlieder/P0045027

cues.title: Return of the cor anglais phrase
cues.text: After Anderson’s lament, the cor anglais plays its opening phrase again. Horns and bowed cellos replace the earlier plucked steps. The song ends on a G major chord, the dominant of its home key, C minor.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 47, Wieder wie zu Anfang and the dominant close. https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler3.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The cor anglais returns with harp
transitions.how: The descending vocal phrase closes in C minor. A ritardando leads into Wie zu Anfang (as at the beginning), and the cor anglais plays its tune again. Harp and plucked double bass now carry the pulse, and the bass clarinet holds a note across the barline.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 40, rehearsal 3; Woltjer, song III, bars 31–33. https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler3.html

transitions.title: Plucked steps, then sustained notes
transitions.to: Coda · Cor anglais, horns and cellos
transitions.how: The cor anglais returns at Wieder wie zu Anfang, accompanied by horn lines and bowed cellos. A ritardando lengthens its last descending phrase. Harp and low strings end on G, and the final G major chord is held under fermatas.

source.title: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, full score (C. F. Kahnt, plate 4460)
source.locator: Song III, printed pp. 33–47: cor anglais and plucked cellos at the opening, harp and double basses in the second stanza. Violins are silent throughout.

timeline.note: Opening: cor anglais and bassoon lines above the pizzicato cello pulse.
Anderson joins the cor anglais and bassoons above plucked cellos.
Harp and plucked double basses replace the cellos beneath the returning cor anglais phrase.
Cor anglais, horns and bowed cellos play the opening material again before the final G-major chord.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor.
